theory.overview: Batch Normalization (BatchNorm) is one of the most important innovations in deep learning. By normalizing layer inputs to have zero mean and unit variance, it dramatically accelerates training, allows higher learning rates, and reduces sensitivity to weight initialization. Introduced by Ioffe & Szegedy in 2015, BatchNorm has become standard in virtually all modern architectures—from ResNet to Transformer. It operates by learning the optimal distribution for each layer, not just forcing standard normal.

sections.title: The Internal Covariate Shift Problem
sections.content: As parameters of preceding layers change during training, the distribution of inputs to subsequent layers changes. This requires constant adaptation and slows learning.
sections.analogy: Like aiming at a moving target—each layer must continuously adjust to new input distributions from previous layers.

sections.title: Normalization Procedure
sections.content: For each feature across the mini-batch:
sections.epsilon: Small constant (1e-5) for numerical stability when variance is near zero
sections.learnable: γ (scale) and β (shift) are learned per feature—allows network to undo normalization if beneficial

sections.title: Training vs Inference
sections.content: Batch statistics are different at training and inference time.
training: Randomness from batch composition adds noise (acts as regularization)
inference: Use fixed running mean and variance (population statistics)
No batch needed—can run single sample

advantages.explanation: Gradients are well-conditioned, less risk of explosion
Networks train from wider range of initial weights
Noise from batch statistics reduces overfitting
ResNet-152, DenseNet-121 would not train without it

sections.title: Placement in Network
sections.content: Where to put BatchNorm? Two common patterns:

patterns.advantage: Works for some architectures (ResNet uses pre-activation variant)

sections.placement: Apply before activation in original, but experiments show both work. Key is consistency.
sections.note: Don't use bias before BatchNorm—it's subtracted out by normalization anyway

sections.title: Variants and Alternatives
sections.content: BatchNorm isn't always ideal. Alternatives for different scenarios:

alternatives.name: Weight Normalization
alternatives.method: Normalize weight vectors instead of activations

sections.smallBatch: BatchNorm degrades with batch size < 8—use GroupNorm or LayerNorm instead

keyConcepts.name: Internal Covariate Shift
keyConcepts.description: Change in distribution of network activations due to parameter updates in previous layers.
keyConcepts.impact: Slows training, requires lower learning rates, makes deep networks hard to train

keyConcepts.name: Learnable Parameters
keyConcepts.description: γ and β allow the network to learn the optimal scale and shift for each layer.
keyConcepts.flexibility: Network can restore original representation if that's optimal: γ=σ, β=μ

keyConcepts.name: Running Statistics
keyConcepts.description: Exponential moving average of mean and variance used at inference time.
keyConcepts.momentum: Typically 0.1—higher = faster adaptation to new statistics

keyConcepts.name: Normalization Dimension
keyConcepts.description: Different normalizations operate across different dimensions:
keyConcepts.batchNorm: Across batch dimension (N, C, H, W) → normalize (N, H, W) per C
keyConcepts.layerNorm: Across feature dimension (C, H, W) per sample

complexity.memory: $O(C)$ for running statistics + $O(N \cdot C \cdot H \cdot W)$ for saved normalized values (backward)
complexity.overhead: Minimal—primarily adds 2 learnable parameters per feature

practiceProblems.title: BatchNorm Dimensions
practiceProblems.description: For CNN activations shaped (N=32, C=64, H=28, W=28), what are the shapes of μ_B, σ²_B, γ, and β?
practiceProblems.answer: All are (64,). Computed per channel across N, H, W dimensions.
practiceProblems.explanation: BatchNorm in CNNs computes statistics per channel. For each of 64 channels: average over all samples (32) and all spatial locations (28×28). Learnable parameters γ and β are also per channel.

practiceProblems.title: Training vs Test Behavior
practiceProblems.description: If you use batch statistics at test time with batch size 1, what happens?
practiceProblems.answer: Normalization fails: μ_B = x_1, σ²_B = 0, so output becomes undefined (division by zero after adding ε).
practiceProblems.explanation: With single sample, mean equals that sample, variance is zero. Normalized value becomes 0/ε which is numerically unstable. This is why running statistics must be used at test time—or BatchNorm layers switched to eval mode.

practiceProblems.title: Learnable Parameters Purpose
practiceProblems.description: Why have learnable γ and β? Why not just normalize to N(0,1) and be done?
practiceProblems.answer: Network may need different distributions. γ=σ_true, β=μ_true restores original if that was optimal. Flexibility is key.
practiceProblems.explanation: If forcing N(0,1) was always best, we'd constrain the network. By learning γ and β, the network discovers what distribution works best. Empirically, networks often learn to maintain some shift and scale rather than pure standard normal.

practiceProblems.title: BatchNorm as Regularization
practiceProblems.description: How does BatchNorm act as a regularizer even without explicit noise injection?
practiceProblems.answer: Batch statistics vary with batch composition. Same sample gets slightly different normalization depending on batchmates—creates noise.
practiceProblems.explanation: μ_B and σ²_B are random variables (functions of which samples happen to be in this batch). This adds noise to activations during training, similar to dropout. Small batches → more variance → stronger regularization.

practiceProblems.title: Small Batch Alternatives
practiceProblems.description: You're training with batch size 4. BatchNorm performs poorly. What alternatives should you consider?
practiceProblems.answer: Use Layer Normalization (per sample), Group Normalization (normalize groups of channels), or Instance Normalization. All work with batch size 1.
practiceProblems.explanation: With batch size 4, batch statistics are too noisy and don't represent population well. LayerNorm normalizes across features per sample—no batch dependence. GroupNorm splits channels into groups and normalizes per group—works for any batch size. These are standard in detection/segmentation where large batches don't fit.
hints: Statistics too noisy with small batch

practiceProblems.title: BatchNorm Before or After Activation
practiceProblems.description: Original paper: BN before activation. ResNet often uses pre-activation (BN-ReLU-Conv). Which is better?
practiceProblems.answer: Both work. Pre-activation (BN-ReLU-Conv) often better for very deep networks—prevents gradient issues in skip connections.
practiceProblems.explanation: Original: Conv-BN-ReLU ensures inputs to next layer are normalized. Pre-activation: BN-ReLU-Conv puts normalization in skip path, helping gradient flow in ResNets. Empirically similar for moderate depth, pre-activation wins for very deep (1000+ layer) networks.

minigame.title: BatchNorm Explorer
minigame.description: Visualize how Batch Normalization stabilizes training. Watch activations distributions shift during training with and without BatchNorm. See the effect of different batch sizes and compare with LayerNorm and GroupNorm.

codeExample.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class BatchNormExample(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_features, momentum=0.1, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_features = num_features
        self.eps = eps
        self.momentum = momentum
        
        # Learnable parameters
        self.gamma = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(num_features))
        self.beta = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(num_features))
        
        # Running statistics (buffers, not parameters)
        self.register_buffer('running_mean', torch.zeros(num_features))
        self.register_buffer('running_var', torch.ones(num_features))
        self.register_buffer('num_batches_tracked', torch.tensor(0, dtype=torch.long))
    
    def forward(self, x):
        if self.training:
            # Compute batch statistics
            # For 2D input: (N, C) - normalize over N
            # For 4D input: (N, C, H, W) - normalize over N, H, W
            
            dim = [0] if x.dim() == 2 else [0, 2, 3]
            batch_mean = x.mean(dim=dim, keepdim=True)
            batch_var = x.var(dim=dim, unbiased=False, keepdim=True)
            
            # Update running statistics
            with torch.no_grad():
                self.running_mean = (1 - self.momentum) * self.running_mean + \n                                    self.momentum * batch_mean.squeeze()
                self.running_var = (1 - self.momentum) * self.running_var + \n                                   self.momentum * batch_var.squeeze()
                self.num_batches_tracked += 1
            
            # Normalize using batch stats
            x_norm = (x - batch_mean) / torch.sqrt(batch_var + self.eps)
        else:
            # Use running statistics
            running_mean = self.running_mean.view(1, -1, *([1] * (x.dim() - 2)))
            running_var = self.running_var.view(1, -1, *([1] * (x.dim() - 2)))
            x_norm = (x - running_mean) / torch.sqrt(running_var + self.eps)
        
        # Scale and shift
        shape = [1, -1] + [1] * (x.dim() - 2)
        return self.gamma.view(shape) * x_norm + self.beta.view(shape)

class ModernCNN(nn.Module):
    """
    CNN with BatchNorm (standard modern architecture)
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels=3, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Conv block 1
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, 64, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(64)
        self.relu1 = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        
        # Conv block 2
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(128)
        self.relu2 = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        
        # Conv block 3
        self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(128, 256, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn3 = nn.BatchNorm2d(256)
        self.relu3 = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        
        # Classifier
        self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(256, num_classes)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        # Block 1
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = self.bn1(x)  # BatchNorm before activation
        x = self.relu1(x)
        
        # Block 2
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = self.bn2(x)
        x = self.relu2(x)
        
        # Block 3
        x = self.conv3(x)
        x = self.bn3(x)
        x = self.relu3(x)
        
        # Classifier
        x = self.pool(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        x = self.fc(x)
        return x

# Different normalization variants
class NormalizationComparison(nn.Module):
    """
    Compare BatchNorm, LayerNorm, GroupNorm, InstanceNorm
    """
    def __init__(self, num_channels=64, num_groups=32):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(num_channels)
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm([num_channels, 28, 28])  # Need spatial dims
        self.gn = nn.GroupNorm(num_groups, num_channels)
        self.in_norm = nn.InstanceNorm2d(num_channels)
    
    def forward(self, x, norm_type='bn'):
        if norm_type == 'bn':
            return self.bn(x)
        elif norm_type == 'ln':
            # LayerNorm: normalize over C, H, W per sample
            return self.ln(x)
        elif norm_type == 'gn':
            return self.gn(x)
        elif norm_type == 'in':
            return self.in_norm(x)

def demonstrate_batchnorm_effects():
    """
    Show how BatchNorm stabilizes training
    """
    print("=== BatchNorm Demonstration ===\n")
    
    # Create sample activations
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    batch_size = 32
    num_features = 64
    
    # Simulate pre-BN: high variance, different scales
    x_before = torch.randn(batch_size, num_features) * torch.linspace(0.1, 5, num_features)
    x_before += torch.linspace(-10, 10, num_features)
    
    print(f'Before BatchNorm:')
    print(f'  Mean range: [{x_before.mean(dim=0).min():.2f}, {x_before.mean(dim=0).max():.2f}]')
    print(f'  Std range: [{x_before.std(dim=0).min():.2f}, {x_before.std(dim=0).max():.2f}]')
    
    # Apply manual BatchNorm
    bn = BatchNormExample(num_features)
    bn.train()
    x_after = bn(x_before.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1))  # Add fake H, W dims
    x_after = x_after.squeeze()
    
    print(f'\nAfter BatchNorm (first batch):')
    print(f'  Mean range: [{x_after.mean(dim=0).min():.2f}, {x_after.mean(dim=0).max():.2f}]')
    print(f'  Std range: [{x_after.std(dim=0).min():.2f}, {x_after.std(dim=0).max():.2f}]')
    
    # After many batches, running stats converge
    for _ in range(100):
        x = torch.randn(batch_size, num_features) * torch.linspace(0.1, 5, num_features)
        x += torch.linspace(-10, 10, num_features)
        _ = bn(x.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1))
    
    # Test mode with running stats
    bn.eval()
    x_test = torch.randn(batch_size, num_features)
    x_test = x_test.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)
    with torch.no_grad():
        x_test_normalized = bn(x_test)
    
    print(f'\nRunning stats after 100 batches:')
    print(f'  Running mean range: [{bn.running_mean.min():.2f}, {bn.running_mean.max():.2f}]')
    print(f'  Running std range: [{torch.sqrt(bn.running_var).min():.2f}, {torch.sqrt(bn.running_var).max():.2f}]')
    
    print(f'\nTest mode output stats:')
    print(f'  Mean: {x_test_normalized.mean().item():.3f}')
    print(f'  Std: {x_test_normalized.std().item():.3f}')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demonstrate_batchnorm_effects()
    
    print(f"\n=== Modern CNN with BatchNorm ===")
    model = ModernCNN(in_channels=3, num_classes=10)
    
    # Count BatchNorm layers
    bn_layers = [m for m in model.modules() if isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d)]
    total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    
    print(f'Number of BatchNorm layers: {len(bn_layers)}')
    print(f'Total parameters: {total_params:,}')
    
    # Test forward pass
    x = torch.randn(4, 3, 224, 224)
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(x)
    print(f'Input: {x.shape} → Output: {output.shape}')
    
    print(f"\n=== Normalization Comparison ===")
    comp = NormalizationComparison(num_channels=64, num_groups=32)
    x = torch.randn(4, 64, 28, 28)
    
    for norm in ['bn', 'ln', 'gn', 'in']:
        try:
            out = comp(x, norm)
            print(f'{norm.upper()}: {x.shape} → {out.shape}')
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'{norm.upper()}: {e}')
